cards.explanation: The answer is bear with them. Paul says the strong ought to bear with the shortcomings of the weak. Bearing with someone means you stay close and carry it with them. And notice he says "we," so he counts himself in with the strong. I've bent a few stamps in my day, so I know how good it feels when somebody is patient with me.

The answer is False. Paul says the strong ought to bear with the shortcomings of the weak “…and not to please ourselves.” Pleasing ourselves first is the thing he steers us away from. He points the strong toward the weak instead. Nobody gets to be first in line at the cooling rack on this one.

The answer is build him up. Paul says to please your neighbor for his good, “…to build him up.” So the goal isn't just making somebody smile for a minute. It's helping him grow stronger. Building up is slow work, friends, like stacking a tall cookie box without crushing the bottom row.

The answer is insults. Paul quotes the words “The insults of those who insult You have fallen on Me.” (Psalm 69:9) He uses them to show that even Christ did not please Himself. I think that's a heavy line, and it's worth sitting with for a second. Jesus took that weight on Himself instead of putting Himself first.

The answer is instruction. Paul says everything written in the past was written for our instruction. So those old words are there to teach us. I read a recipe so I can bake the thing, not so I can frame the page. Paul goes on to say that through endurance and the encouragement of the Scriptures, we might have hope.

The answer is glorify. Paul asks God to grant harmony so that with one mind and one voice you may glorify “…the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.” One mind and one voice, friends, and not a single person sneaking in a different song. The harmony points to God.

The answer is Christ. Paul says to accept one another, then, just as Christ accepted you. Christ is the measuring stick, and Paul doesn't put himself up there. Honestly, I'd be nervous if my name were the standard. I can't even stamp a straight line some days.
The answer is True. Paul says accepting one another is “…in order to bring glory to God.” So it isn't only about getting along. It brings glory to God. He ties it back to Christ, who accepted you.

The answer is the Gentiles. Paul says Christ became a servant “…so that the Gentiles may glorify God for His mercy.” The Gentiles are people who aren't Jews. Mercy is what this part is about. Paul wants them praising God for it.

The answer is His people. The quote says “Rejoice, O Gentiles, with His people.” So the Gentiles aren't rejoicing off in a corner by themselves. They're rejoicing together with God's people. Paul is showing both groups in one celebration.

The answer is False. The quote says “Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles, and extol Him, all you peoples.” It's all the Gentiles and all the peoples, not only some. When a verse says all twice in one breath, I don't go hunting for exceptions.

The answer is put their hope. Isaiah's words are “in Him the Gentiles will put their hope.” Their hope rests in Him, the Root of Jesse. That's what Paul has been building toward: the Gentiles have a real place to put their hope.

The answer is the Holy Spirit. Paul says you may overflow with hope “…by the power of the Holy Spirit.” The power behind the overflow is the Spirit's. And friends, overflow is the word, like a cookie jar nobody can close.
